news.content_title: 18,566 Norovirus Food Poisoning Patients the Following Winter | Translating Staff Attendance Decisions, Process Exclusion, and Vomit Cleanup into Decision Tables and Record Formats|今城 敏(Satoshi Imanari)
news.content: メインコンテンツへスキップ 18,566 Norovirus Food Poisoning Patients the Following Winter | Translating Staff Attendance Decisions, Process Exclusion, and Vomit Cleanup into Decision Tables and Record Formats 返金可 今城 敏(Satoshi Imanari) Oct 29, 2026 19:00 What should be left on-site during the norovirus epidemic season is a record of who decided whether to have a staff member with poor physical condition "come to work," "remove them from which process," and "when to return them," based on what they observed, as well as records of procedures, materials, and training for cleaning up vomit. Let's start with the numbers. According to A4 of the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare's "Q&A on Norovirus," in 2025, there were 462 norovirus food poisoning incidents out of a total of 1,172 (39.4%), and 18,566 patients out of a total of 24,727 (75.1%) (figures updated as of June 30, 2026). This is the highest number of patients in the 10-year period from 2016 to 2025 shown in the same table. A8 of the same Q&A explains that although outbreaks occur throughout the year, the number of cases tends to start increasing around November, peaking from December to January of the following year. [Imajo's Practical Proposal] Since the peak varies from year to year, I recommend setting up the system on the premise of maintaining the same structure from November to March. There is another figure related to how causes are identified. A13 of the same Q&A states that in about 70% of norovirus food poisoning cases, the causative food is not identified, and the reason for this is that in many cases, food is contaminated via food handlers infected with the virus. This is why you should solidify personnel management before chasing after causative foods. Why it matters to your company [Scientific Knowledge] A18 of the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare's "Q&A on Norovirus" explains that in food poisoning caused by norovirus, there are many cases where the patient's feces or vomit contaminated food through humans, and because infection occurs with a small amount of virus, even food with a very small amount of feces or vomit attached can cause many people to develop symptoms. [Official Recommendation] The same A18 recommends that food handlers report to the person in charge of the cooking facility, etc. (business operator, food hygiene supervisor, etc.) if they have symptoms such as diarrhea, vomiting, or cold-like symptoms. The same A18 indicates that "the person in charge of the cooking facility, etc., should not allow persons with symptoms such as diarrhea or vomiting to engage in work that directly handles food" (Source: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare "Q&A on Norovirus" Q18/A18). The Q&A is an administrative explanatory document and is positioned differently from laws and regulations that have legal binding force. This applies to food factories, school lunches, and delicatessen production sites that have staff who directly handle food. [Imajo's Practical Proposal] I recommend including departments that do not directly touch food, such as packaging of pre-packaged products, shipping, warehousing, and administration, in the health check target because they share toilets, break rooms, and doorknobs, but changing only the judgment for exclusion from the process based on the classification. [Imajo's Practical Proposal] I recommend documenting in-house how many days to exclude someone and which processes are considered "work that directly handles food." This is to prevent conclusions from changing based on the intuition of the site leader on that day. There is one point that is easily overlooked. It is how to handle the situation after symptoms have subsided. The Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare Q&A A18 states that even after symptoms such as diarrhea have subsided, virus shedding can continue for about one week, and sometimes up to one month. The Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare "Q&A on Norovirus" A5 explains that norovirus infection is a part of "infectious gastroenteritis," which is classified as a Category V infectious disease. [Imajo's Practical Proposal] I recommend preparing for the judgment of exclusion and return on the premise that the hygiene manager will make the decision using the company's own judgment table, without waiting for contact from the government. When you line up official documents and laws, you can see the difference in strength and specificity. [Legal Obligation] 21 CFR §117.10(a) in the United States requires that persons who have a reasonable possibility of contaminating food, etc., due to illness, etc., be excluded from operations where there is a risk of contamination until the condition is corrected, with the exception of cases where open wounds, etc., are properly covered with impermeable coverings, etc. [Imajo's Practical Proposal] For factories exporting to the U.S., if you keep your domestic judgment table in a form that can be used as an explanation for U.S. CGMP, you can handle FDA inspections and client audits with a single explanation. I will write down the reasons for dealing with this now, categorized by the type of deadline. Epidemic season guidelines (trends in administrative statistics): "The number of cases starts to increase around November, and the peak of outbreaks is from December to January of the following year" from the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare Q&A A8. [Imajo's Practical Proposal] In-house deadline: Decide on the judgment table and record format by 17:00 (JST) on Friday, November 13, 2026, and conduct one training session on vomit cleanup by 17:00 (JST) on Monday, November 30, 2026. トップ 健康・医療 病気 あなたへのおすすめ ここから先は 3,647字/2画像 記事¥500 購入手続きへ ログイン

Why it matters to your company [Scientific Knowledge] A18 of the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare's "Q&A on Norovirus" explains that in food poisoning caused by norovirus, there are many cases where the patient's feces or vomit contaminated food through humans, and because infection occurs with a small amount of virus, even food with a very small amount of feces or vomit attached can cause many people to develop symptoms. [Official Recommendation] The same A18 recommends that food handlers report to the person in charge of the cooking facility, etc. (business operator, food hygiene supervisor, etc.) if they have symptoms such as diarrhea, vomiting, or cold-like symptoms. The same A18 indicates that "the person in charge of the cooking facility, etc., should not allow persons with symptoms such as diarrhea or vomiting to engage in work that directly handles food" (Source: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare "Q&A on Norovirus" Q18/A18). The Q&A is an administrative explanatory document and is positioned differently from laws and regulations that have legal binding force. This applies to food factories, school lunches, and delicatessen production sites that have staff who directly handle food. [Imajo's Practical Proposal] I recommend including departments that do not directly touch food, such as packaging of pre-packaged products, shipping, warehousing, and administration, in the health check target because they share toilets, break rooms, and doorknobs, but changing only the judgment for exclusion from the process based on the classification. [Imajo's Practical Proposal] I recommend documenting in-house how many days to exclude someone and which processes are considered "work that directly handles food." This is to prevent conclusions from changing based on the intuition of the site leader on that day. There is one point that is easily overlooked. It is how to handle the situation after symptoms have subsided. The Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare Q&A A18 states that even after symptoms such as diarrhea have subsided, virus shedding can continue for about one week, and sometimes up to one month. The Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare "Q&A on Norovirus" A5 explains that norovirus infection is a part of "infectious gastroenteritis," which is classified as a Category V infectious disease. [Imajo's Practical Proposal] I recommend preparing for the judgment of exclusion and return on the premise that the hygiene manager will make the decision using the company's own judgment table, without waiting for contact from the government. When you line up official documents and laws, you can see the difference in strength and specificity. [Legal Obligation] 21 CFR §117.10(a) in the United States requires that persons who have a reasonable possibility of contaminating food, etc., due to illness, etc., be excluded from operations where there is a risk of contamination until the condition is corrected, with the exception of cases where open wounds, etc., are properly covered with impermeable coverings, etc. [Imajo's Practical Proposal] For factories exporting to the U.S., if you keep your domestic judgment table in a form that can be used as an explanation for U.S. CGMP, you can handle FDA inspections and client audits with a single explanation. I will write down the reasons for dealing with this now, categorized by the type of deadline. Epidemic season guidelines (trends in administrative statistics): "The number of cases starts to increase around November, and the peak of outbreaks is from December to January of the following year" from the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare Q&A A8. [Imajo's Practical Proposal] In-house deadline: Decide on the judgment table and record format by 17:00 (JST) on Friday, November 13, 2026, and conduct one training session on vomit cleanup by 17:00 (JST) on Monday, November 30, 2026. トップ 健康・医療 病気 あなたへのおすすめ ここから先は 3,647字/2画像 記事¥500 購入手続きへ ログイン

news.content_title: Shared Dipping Sauce Can Spread Oral Bacteria and Norovirus, Food Safety Research Shows
news.content: News Issues Wellness Beauty Pharma KOREAN SEARCH Search Health Chosun Shared Dipping Sauce Can Spread Oral Bacteria and Norovirus, Food Safety Research Shows by Kim Bo Mi Updated 2026/10/30 04:30 When eating with other people, it is best to use a separate sauce bowl whenever possible. /AI-generated image When eating with other people, use a separate sauce bowl. Oral bacteria can be transferred, and caution is needed because norovirus infection is also possible. According to the ‘Journal of Food Safety,’ dipping food into sauce more than once increases the number of bacteria in the sauce. Researchers compared a group that dipped crackers into sterile water and put them in their mouths with a group that put the crackers in their mouths before dipping them into sterile water. The number of bacteria in the solution was significantly higher when the crackers were put in the mouth before being dipped into the sterile water. Dipping crackers into sterile water just 3 to 6 times transferred about 10,000 bacteria from the mouth. In a real-world situation, when crackers are dipped into sauce twice, an average of 50 to 100 bacteria can be transferred from person to person in a single bite, depending on the size of the sauce bowl and the sauce’s consistency. The researchers said, “Dipping food twice carries the risk of transferring oral bacteria to the food,” adding, “Avoiding this behavior can help prevent the spread of harmful microorganisms to some extent.” Using the same sauce bowl can increase the risk of norovirus infection. /AI-generated image Sharing the same sauce bowl does not always lead to a serious illness, but norovirus can be transmitted. Benjamin Chapman, a professor in the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences at North Carolina State University, said in an interview with ‘The Washington Post,’ “Pathogens that cause colds are transmitted through coughing and sneezing rather than through food or drinks, but norovirus can spread through direct contact such as shaking hands, contaminated food and water, aerosols, and saliva.” Norovirus is highly contagious. People with symptoms should use separate utensils. /AI-generated image People infected with norovirus can release billions of norovirus particles through feces or vomit. The virus is so contagious that just 18 particles can infect another person. If you have diarrhea or vomiting, do not handle food with your bare hands or share utensils with others. The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, CDC, said caution is needed because people can continue to spread the virus for more than 2 weeks after their symptoms improve. After eating, wash utensils with hot water and detergent. If washing dishes is not possible, using disposable items is another option. Discard food touched by the patient or contaminated with vomit. Disinfect items that the patient has touched, excluding utensils, with a solution of bleach and water diluted at a ratio of 50:1. news.content: Skip to content MyUCSC People Calendars Maps A-Z Index Search News Explore topics Arts & Culture Climate & Sustainability Earth & Space Health Social Justice & Community Student Experience Technology News by Division Arts Engineering Humanities Science Social Sciences On Campus For Journalists Media Coverage Events Home Health How a gut virus hijacks mucus production to slip past the body’s protective barrier New study reveals how astroviruses use goblet cells as an escape route from the small intestines to evade host immunity and enhance spread and transmission, presenting a new path for treating pediatric diarrhea. November 3, 2026 Mike Peña UC Santa Cruz graduate student Melanie Kirkpatrick, seated, prepares to purify mucin from cells with guidance from fellow graduate student Michelle Pablo (wearing white) and Professor Valerie Cortez. Credit: Cortez Lab Press Inquiries Press Contact Mike Peña mivpena@ucsc.edu (831) 459-4352 Key takeaways This study reveals a unique and stealthy exit strategy used by astroviruses. Rotavirus and norovirus, which also infect the small intestines, are known to break through the organ’s inner lining in order to increase spread within the body and among other hosts. In mouse and human cell-culture models, the research team found that blocking mucus secretion reduced virus release, while stimulating it increased virus levels—revealing astrovirus’s escape route. Uncovering this exit mechanism provides potential new targets for developing treatments against pediatric diarrhea, a leading cause of death for children around the world under the age of 5. Among the various viruses that sicken your gut, some at least leave behind a tiny path of cellular destruction as they replicate, implicating the guilty pathogen. Both rotavirus and norovirus invade the small intestines, multiply there, and can break through the organ’s outer lining as one way of proliferating in the body. Astroviruses, which infect the same organ and cause pediatric diarrhea worldwide, have a slicker strategy that avoids tissue damage. In a new study published in the Proceedings of the Library of Science: Pathogens, a team of cell biologists at the University of California, Santa Cruz, report the astrovirus’s exit strategy. In a few words, it can be summed up as, “follow the mucus.” The team discovered that astrovirus relies on mucus secretion from goblet cells as the coordinated path to completing its replication cycle. The finding reveals potentially new targets for strategies to treat pediatric diarrhea, according to the paper’s senior author, Valerie Cortez, a professor of molecular, cell, and developmental biology at UC Santa Cruz. “Together, these findings highlight a new facet of enteric virus-host biology that allows for the efficient release of virus particles,” Cortez said. “Prior to our study, the pathway by which astroviruses exit the cell was largely unknown, unlike for other major enteric viruses like norovirus and rotavirus.” Gaining on a deadly virus The study builds on the Cortez Lab‘s previous discovery that astrovirus targets the intestine’s goblet cells. The single-stranded RNA virus infects birds and mammals, and in humans, is a major driver of pediatric diarrhea—especially in parts of the world with poor water access. Globally, diarrhea is a leading cause of death for children under the age of 5. Goblet cells create a thin layer of mucus that insulates the intestinal wall, which keeps most microbes, pathogens, and whatever we ingest from seeping into the rest of the body, according to the study’s lead author, Natalie Pedicino. How astrovirus gets past this protective system, and indeed leverages it, was the focus of Pedicino’s Ph.D. thesis in the Cortez Lab. This viscous process was also the subject of a lightning talk Pedicino gave in 2024 that took her to the UC-wide Grad Slam championship, where Ph.D. students from each campus competed for top honors by distilling their research into a presentation of three minutes or less. Pedicino’s talk was titled, “From Mucus Factory to Virus Factory: A Novel Gut Virus’ Global Impact on Children.” Pedicino’s first-place presentation at the campus-level Grad Slam contest in March 2024 at the Santa Cruz Kuumbwa Jazz Center. “We discovered this novel mechanism where astrovirus essentially hijacks goblet cells,” Pedicino said. “This finding is exciting, both for the field of astrovirus research and for gut viruses as a whole because it reveals another viral exit strategy.” Exit route equals new possibilities The team used both mouse and human cell-culture models to see if mucus served as a path for astrovirus to exit from goblet cells and spread. When they blocked mucus secretion, it reduced the level of virus release. When they stimulated mucus secretion, virus levels increased. Identifying this mechanism has broader implications for cellular processes that allow certain viruses to evade host immunity and enhance spread and transmission. Purified mucin, a protein that serves as the main component of mucus, where Cortez’s team identified astrovirus (in red). For example, Cortez explained that “hiding” in mucus could help a virus avoid detection or enhance entry into new cells, similar to how rotavirus and norovirus form membrane-cloaked clusters to slip into a cell. Previous studies have shown that mucus stabilizes the temperature of human astrovirus, perhaps aiding its spread within and between hosts. “This discovery identifies a unique exit strategy for an enteric virus that allows it to spread without having to bust open and kill its host cell,” Cortez said. “Understanding this host-virus interaction during the replication cycle can provide new insights into pathogenesis and potentially new targets for treatment strategies that prevent astrovirus spread.” Career trajectories and collaboration Pedicino, the Cortez Lab’s first Ph.D. graduate, is now a tenure-track biology instructor at West Valley College in Saratoga, Calif. Co-authors Jacob Gulman and Nicole Heredia-Osuna are former UC Santa Cruz undergraduates who worked as research specialists in Cortez’s lab. Gulman and Heredia-Osuna are now in graduate programs, respectively, at Stony Brook University and University of Nevada, Reno. The team also collaborated with researchers at the Baskin School of Engineering. Rebecca DuBois, professor of biomolecular engineering, and her graduate student Adam Lentz shared reagents with the Cortez Lab, including purified human astrovirus spike protein and engineered antibodies that detect human astrovirus. UC Santa Cruz’s Flow Cytometry Core, Microscopy Center, and Vivarium played critical roles for this study, which was funded by a Maximizing Investigators’ Research Award that Cortez received earlier this year from the National Institutes of Health. analysis.time: The study was published on November 3, 2026. The research findings were based on experiments conducted in mouse and human cell-culture models, with the thesis work focused on the 2024 Grad Slam contest.
analysis.location_and_population: The research was conducted at the University of California, Santa Cruz, and involves human and mouse cell-culture models. Astroviruses infect the small intestines of humans, particularly in regions with poor water access, and cause pediatric diarrhea globally.
analysis.event: A study published by UC Santa Cruz researchers revealed how astroviruses use mucus secretion from goblet cells as an exit strategy to evade host immunity and enhance transmission. This discovery was reported by the UC Santa Cruz News and supported by experimental results from cell-culture models.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Astroviruses are a major driver of pediatric diarrhea in humans, especially in areas with poor water access. The study highlights a unique mechanism that allows the virus to spread without damaging its host cell, which could have implications for treatment strategies. However, no specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers were reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study was conducted using mouse and human cell-culture models, and the findings were confirmed through experimental results. The research team identified the astrovirus’s exit strategy and its implications for treatment, but no further details on public health responses or ongoing investigations were provided.

analysis.brief_en: A new study from UC Santa Cruz reveals how astroviruses use mucus secretion from goblet cells as an exit strategy to evade host immunity and enhance transmission. Published on November 3, 2026, the research, led by graduate student Natalie Pedicino, demonstrates that blocking mucus secretion reduces virus release, while stimulating it increases virus levels. This discovery, based on experiments with mouse and human cell-culture models, highlights a unique mechanism that allows astroviruses to spread without damaging their host cells. The findings could lead to new treatment strategies for pediatric diarrhea, a leading cause of death for children under 5 globally. The study builds on previous work by the Cortez Lab, which identified astrovirus’s targeting of goblet cells. While the research provides insights into viral exit strategies, no specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers were reported in the supplied evidence. The study was funded by the National Institutes of Health and involved collaboration with other researchers at UC Santa Cruz.

news.source_body_en: A new study from UC Santa Cruz reveals how astroviruses use mucus secretion from goblet cells as an exit strategy to evade host immunity and enhance transmission. Published on November 3, 2026, the research, led by graduate student Natalie Pedicino, demonstrates that blocking mucus secretion reduces virus release, while stimulating it increases virus levels. This discovery, based on experiments with mouse and human cell-culture models, highlights a unique mechanism that allows astroviruses to spread without damaging their host cells. The findings could lead to new treatment strategies for pediatric diarrhea, a leading cause of death for children under 5 globally. The study builds on previous work by the Cortez Lab, which identified astrovirus’s targeting of goblet cells. While the research provides insights into viral exit strategies, no specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers were reported in the supplied evidence. news.content_zh: 加州大学圣克鲁斯分校的一项新研究揭示了星状病毒如何利用杯状细胞的粘液分泌作为逃避 宿主 免疫并增强 传播 的退出策略。这项由研究生 Natalie Pedicino 领导的研究于 2026 年 11 月 3 日发表,表明阻止粘液分泌会减少病毒释放,而刺激粘液分泌会增加病毒水平。这一发现基于小鼠和人类细胞培养模型的实验,强调了一种独特的机制,可以让星状病毒在不损害其 宿主 细胞的情况下传播。这些发现可能会导致针对小儿腹泻的新 治疗 策略,小儿腹泻是全球 5 岁以下儿童死亡的主要原因。这项研究建立在 Cortez 实验室之前的工作基础上,该实验室确定了星状病毒对杯状细胞的靶向作用。虽然该研究提供了对病毒退出策略的见解,但所提供的证据中没有报告具体的病例数、死亡数或暴露数量。该研究由美国国立卫生研究院资助,并与加州大学圣克鲁斯分校的其他研究人员合作。

news.content: 站内 近期高发,内蒙古疾控中心最新提示 城市速递 2026年10月30日 12:29:10 来自北京市 诺如病毒胃肠炎是由诺如病毒(Norovirus,NoV)感染引起的急性消化道传染病,具有高度传染性和快速传播能力。诺如病毒感染是引起急性胃肠炎暴发的主要原因之一,全年可发生,冬春季高发,易在封闭、人群密集的场所暴发。 诺如病毒在外环境中稳定,在pH2.7的液体中3小时,地下水、冷藏和冷冻食品中数月后仍具有感染性。普通自来水中的游离氯、75%乙醇、60°C30分钟等对诺如病毒作用有限。高浓度(1000-5000mg/L)含氯消毒剂作用1-5分钟、85°C以上至少1分钟可完全灭活诺如病毒。 患者和无症状感染者是主要传染源 感染者在潜伏期末开始排毒,在出现症状后的24-48小时内达到高峰,排毒时间可持续2-3周,免疫功能低下者可长达数月。人群普遍易感,婴幼儿、老年人、免疫功能低下、营养不良人群感染后更易发病。 主要通过粪-口途径传播 与感染者密切接触或接触含诺如病毒的吐泻物或被病毒污染的环境或物品,摄入被诺如病毒污染的食物或水均可造成传播。特定条件下,如冲洗呕吐物、粪便时飞溅产生的气溶胶,大量吸入也可感染。 主要防护建议 1.加强学生健康管理。严格落实晨午检制度、因病缺勤登记及病因追访制度。一旦发现学生、教职工等出现呕吐、腹泻等症状,应立即引导其就医。发现因病缺勤异常增多时,立即报告主管部门。 2.保障饮用水安全卫生。加强校园饮用水设施管理,重点排查供水管网破损、渗漏等隐患,确保供水系统安全无污染。 3.加强食品卫生与从业人员健康管理。严格规范食材采购、储存及加工流程,落实生熟分开,确保食物烧熟煮透;强化食堂从业人员健康状况监测,制作食物和配餐过程需戴口罩并做好手卫生,出现呕吐、腹泻等症状,应立即暂停工作,及时就医。 4.做好环境清洁消毒工作。对教室、宿舍、食堂、图书馆、卫生间等公共区域定期清洁与通风。对门把手、楼梯扶手、水龙头、电梯按钮、上下床扶手等高频接触物体表面定期清洁与消毒。 5.规范处置呕吐物。发现患者呕吐物和粪便,应由经过规范培训的人员按照相关操作指引规范处理。重点对被呕吐物或粪便污染的环境物体表面、生活用品、食品加工工具、生活饮用水等进行消毒。 6.加强健康教育宣传。开学季利用班会、致家长一封信等形式开展诺如病毒防控知识宣教,让学生养成勤洗手、吃熟食、喝开水的良好卫生习惯。 送你新闻盲盒 选一个拆开吧 来源 丨内蒙古疾控 编辑丨张国军 值班主任丨格根哈斯 审核丨王雪仙 张群群 李涛 点亮“ ”和“ ” 给小布加个鸡腿吧 本文来自大风号,仅代表大风号自媒体观点。 凤凰V现场 独家对话深蓝CEO姜海荣:大模型上车,车机正在告别“听指令” 德国IFA直击:中国企业如何用AI读懂一个家?2026中国联通合作伙伴大会在上海举行,九大成果看联通智能化布局华为Mate XT 2展翼三折叠深度体验:三折叠的新答案IFA 2026 ,安克硬控全场查看更多

source_language_evidence.brief_en: 站内 近期高发,内蒙古疾控中心最新提示 城市速递 2026年10月30日 12:29:10 来自北京市 诺如病毒胃肠炎是由诺如病毒(Norovirus,NoV)感染引起的急性消化道传染病,具有高度传染性和快速传播能力。诺如病毒感染是引起急性胃肠炎暴发的主要原因之一,全年可发生,冬春季高发,易在封闭、人群密集的场所暴发。 诺如病毒在外环境中稳定,在pH2.7的液体中3小时,地下水、冷藏和冷冻食品中数月后仍具有感染性。普通自来水中的游离氯、75%乙醇、60°C30分钟等对诺如病毒作用有限。高浓度(1000-5000mg/L)含氯消毒剂作用1-5分钟、85°C以上至少1分钟可完全灭活诺如病毒。 患者和无症状感染者是主要传染源 感染者在潜伏期末开始排毒,在出现症状后的24-48小时内达到高峰,排毒时间可持续2-3周,免疫功能低下者可长达数月。人群普遍易感,婴幼儿、老年人、免疫功能低下、营养不良人群感染后更易发病。 主要通过粪-口途径传播 与感染者密切接触或接触含诺如病毒的吐泻物或被病毒污染的环境或物品,摄入被诺如病毒污染的食物或水均可造成传播。特定条件下,如冲洗呕吐物、粪便时飞溅产生的气溶胶,大量吸入也可感染。 主要防护建议 1.加强学生健康管理。严格落实晨午检制度、因病缺勤登记及病因追访制度。一旦发现学生、教职工等出现呕吐、腹泻等症状,应立即引导其就医。发现因病缺勤异常增多时,立即报告主管部门。 2.保障饮用水安全卫生。加强校园饮用水设施管理,重点排查供水管网破损、渗漏等隐患,确保供水系统安全无污染。 3.加强食品卫生与从业人员健康管理。严格规范食材采购、储存及加工流程,落实生熟分开,确保食物烧熟煮透;强化食堂从业人员健康状况监测,制作食物和配餐过程需戴口罩并做好手卫生,出现呕吐、腹泻等症状,应立即暂停工作,及时就医。

supplementary_news.excerpt: 半夜,孩子突然吐了。 家长忙着换床单、擦地板,又赶紧端来一大杯水。还没忙完,脑子里已经冒出几个问题: 秋冬季出现突然呕吐、腹泻,需要警惕诺如病毒感染。但上吐下泻不一定都是诺如病毒,病因仍需结合具体情况判断。 面对这类症状,家庭首先要做好两件事:照顾患者,减少传播。 诺如病毒感染常表现为恶心、呕吐、腹痛和腹泻,也可能伴有发热。儿童往往呕吐更突出,成人则常以腹泻为主。 它可以通过被污染的食物、水和物品 ...
